I have been working this land since I was twenty years old. I know what Quzhou's soil needs, what the weather usually brings, and how much my body and my family can manage. Some of my children work in the city now, so I have fewer hands. I have to be practical.

My 18 mu I split the way I always have: about 10 mu for cotton — that is the money crop, the one I know best — and the other 8 mu I put into wheat and maize in rotation. Same land, same rotation I have done for thirty years. Wheat goes in this autumn, maize follows after wheat harvest next summer.

For cotton, I will plough deep in spring the way my mother taught me, then plant improved seed from the county supply station — I stopped using my own saved seed years ago after the yield dropped. Cotton drinks a lot of water and draws every pest in the county, so I irrigate five times and spray for bollworm and aphids at least six times. I do not cut corners on cotton pesticides. One bad outbreak and the whole season is gone.

For wheat, I use rotary tillage and improved seed. I irrigate three times — once before winter, once at jointing, once at heading. I apply urea in two splits because my neighbor's son told me that's better and I tried it, it worked, so I kept it.

For maize I do not till at all. I plant straight into the wheat stubble with a simple seeder my son borrowed once. Hybrid seed gives better yield, everybody uses it now. Maize mostly rains well enough here in summer so I only irrigate twice if it is dry.

I am not young, I cannot do heavy work every day. So I choose methods I can manage myself or with occasional help from my grandchildren on weekends.
